c:T6cf,# Label Consensus: editorial

**Pattern.** Majority element (Boyer-Moore vote), with a hash-map counting solution as the baseline.

**Brute force.** Count every label against every other: O(n^2), roughly 4 * 10^10 comparisons at the limit.

**Hash-map baseline (O(n) time, O(n) space).** Count each label, then return the one whose count exceeds `n / 2`.
This is a fully acceptable answer in an interview. State the space cost, then offer to do better.

**Key observation.** Pair off two *different* labels and throw both away. A strict majority label outnumbers all
the others combined, so it can never be cancelled completely: it is the only label that can survive.

**Algorithm (O(n) time, O(1) space).** Keep a `candidate` and a `votes` counter. For each label: if `votes == 0`
take it as the candidate; add one when it matches, subtract one when it does not. The survivor is the only
*possible* winner. A **second pass** counts it and checks `2 * count > n`; otherwise print `-1`.

**Complexity.** Two passes: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

**Pitfalls.** Skipping the confirmation pass (the survivor of `1 2 3` is `3`, which is no majority). Reporting the
most common label even when it has only a plurality. Using `>= n / 2` (a tie is not a majority) or integer
division with odd `n`. Reading labels into 32-bit ints.

**Follow-ups.** Elements appearing more than `n / 3` times: Misra-Gries with two candidates. Streaming labels:
the same counter works online, but confirming needs a second pass or a stored count. Weighted annotators:
replace `+1` / `-1` with weights. In ML terms this is the consensus rule used to aggregate noisy labels before
training; real pipelines usually use annotator-quality models rather than a hard majority.

2d:I[97367,["$2"],"OutletBoundary"]
2f:I[27201,["$2"],"IconMark"]
e:T653,# Batch Packer: editorial

**Pattern.** Binary search on the answer, with a greedy feasibility check.

**Brute force (O(b * n^2)).** `dp[j][i]` = best largest-batch cost splitting the first `i` sequences
into `j` batches; transition over the last cut. Correct, and the way to validate the fast solution on
small inputs. It is far too slow for `n = 2 * 10^5`.

**Key observation.** Ask the easier question: "can I do it with every batch costing at most `cap`?"
Pack greedily: keep adding sequences to the current batch until the next would overflow, then start a new
batch. Greedy is optimal for the check because ending a batch later never hurts a later batch. If
the batch count is at most `b`, `cap` is feasible. Feasibility is **monotone** in `cap`, so the smallest
feasible `cap` can be found by binary search.

**Bounds.** The answer is at least `max(len)` (a sequence cannot be split) and at most `sum(len)` (one
batch). That is about 31 iterations of an O(n) check: O(n log(sum)).

**Pitfalls.** Starting the low bound at 0 or 1 makes the check accept a `cap` smaller than a single
sequence. Using 32-bit integers for the sum (it reaches 2 * 10^14). The "average" shortcut
`ceil(total / b)` ignores order and is only a lower bound. Off-by-one in the loop (`lo < hi` with
`hi = mid`, or `lo <= hi` with `hi = mid - 1`; stay consistent).

**Follow-ups.** The same shape solves "ship packages within D days" and "split array largest sum".
Sequences can be reordered: this becomes bin packing (NP-hard), so discuss first-fit-decreasing.
Minimise the number of batches for a given cap: that is just the greedy count.

10:T4d5,# Context Window: editorial

**Pattern.** Variable-size sliding window (two pointers) with a frequency map.

**Brute force (O(n^2)).** For each start, extend right while the distinct count is at most `k`.
Correct, and the right first answer to state; it fails the perf group.

**Sliding window (O(n)).** Move `right` one step at a time and count the new id. While the window
has more than `k` distinct ids, move `left` forward, decrementing counts and **erasing an id when its
count hits zero**. After the shrink the window is valid, so record `right - left + 1`. Each index
enters and leaves the window once, so the total work is linear even though there is a nested loop.

**Why it is correct.** Cheap spans are closed under shrinking: if `[l, r]` is cheap then so is every
sub-span. So when `left` is advanced past an invalid start it never needs to move back.

**Pitfalls.** Forgetting to erase zero counts (the map size never drops). Clearing the whole window
when it overflows instead of shrinking from the left. Using an array indexed by id (ids reach 10^9).

**Follow-ups.** Longest span with at most `k` distinct ids *replacing* up to `m` tokens. Return the
span itself. The stream is unbounded: keep only the window in memory.

12:T7d1,# Fewest Tokens: editorial

**Pattern.** 1D dynamic programming over prefixes (word-break family, minimising a count).

**Brute force.** Try every piece at every position recursively. Without memoisation the same suffix is solved
many times: exponential in `|s|`. It is the specification for the small tests only.

**Greedy trap.** Always taking the longest matching piece is tempting (real BPE-style tokenizers do apply
merges greedily) but it is *not* optimal for this question. With pieces `ab`, `abc`, `cd` and the text `abcd`, the longest
first piece `abc` leaves a `d` that nothing matches, while `ab` + `cd` spells the whole text.

**State.** `best[i]` = the fewest pieces that spell the first `i` characters, `INF` if impossible; `best[0] = 0`.

**Transition.** `best[i] = min(best[i - len] + 1)` over every length `len` (1 to the longest piece) where
`s[i - len, i)` is a piece **and** `best[i - len]` is reachable. Only lengths up to the longest piece need checking.

**Complexity.** `L` is the longest piece (at most 8): O(n * L) substring lookups in a hash set, about O(n * L^2)
character work; O(n) space. Iterating over all `m` pieces per position instead costs O(n * m * L), roughly 3 * 10^9
at the limits, too slow.

**Pitfalls.** Treating unreachable prefixes as `0` (they then look free: print `-1` by checking `INF`, never by a
sentinel that arithmetic can reach). Forgetting `len <= i`. Returning the number of characters instead of pieces.
Using plain recursion for `n = 2 * 10^5`: depth and time both blow up.

**Follow-ups.** Count the number of segmentations modulo a prime. Recover one optimal split (store the previous
index). Use a trie so a lookup never builds substrings. Weighted pieces (cost per token, as in a pricing model) turn
the `+ 1` into `+ cost`. Compare with how production tokenizers actually work: they apply learned merge rules
rather than solving this optimisation, so the minimum-token split is an upper bound on efficiency, not what a
tokenizer returns.

14:T4cc,# Hot Tokens: editorial

**Pattern.** Frequency counting followed by top-k selection.

**Approach 1: count and sort (O(d log d)).** Count with a hash map, put the `d` distinct tokens in a
vector, sort by (count desc, id asc) and take `k`. Correct and often fast enough; mention it first.

**Approach 2: count and a size-k heap (O(n + d log k)).** Keep a min-heap of the best `k` seen so
far, with the *worst* candidate on top: lower count is worse, and on equal counts the larger id is
worse. Push every token, pop when the size passes `k`. The heap is smaller than the map when
`k << d`.

**Approach 3: bucket by count (O(n)).** Counts are at most `n`, so bucket tokens by count and walk
from the highest bucket down, sorting each bucket by id. Linear, with more code.

**Pitfalls.** The tie-break direction inverts when you move from "sort descending" to "heap with the
worst on top". A quadratic count per element passes small tests and fails the perf group.  Ids
reach 10^9, so keep them in `long long` (or `int` only if you never add them).

**Follow-ups.** The stream never ends: use a count-min sketch plus a heap, or the Misra-Gries
summary, and state the error bound. Ties are weighted by recency: change the heap key.

203716258 203734349 203761379 203792547 203838450 203848240 203897270 203911554 203911794 203913702 203923416 203947931 203960116 203965570 203994404 204018782 204050167 204068422 204078305 204088998 20410790217:T646,# Pipeline Order: editorial

**Pattern.** Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) with a min-heap for the tie-break.

**Brute force (O(n! * m)).** Try permutations in lexicographic order and return the first one that
respects every pair. It is the specification, and it is how the fast solution is validated on tiny inputs.

**Key observation.** A stage can run when every prerequisite has finished, i.e. its unfinished-prerequisite
count is 0. Running a stage lowers the counts of the stages that depend on it. To get the lexicographically
smallest order, always run the smallest ready label: picking any larger ready stage first could only make the
first differing position bigger. Keep the ready labels in a min-heap.

**Cycle.** Stages on a cycle never reach count 0, so the order ends up shorter than `n`: print `-1`.
A self-loop `a a` is the smallest cycle; duplicate pairs just count twice and are decremented twice.

**Complexity.** Each stage enters and leaves the heap once and each pair is touched once:
O((n + m) log n) time, O(n + m) space.

**Pitfalls.** A FIFO queue gives a valid but not the smallest order. Forgetting the cycle check prints a
short answer. Scanning for the smallest ready stage is O(n^2). Using a DFS post-order needs the reverse and
does not give the smallest order directly.

**Follow-ups.** Largest order instead: a max-heap. "Which stages can run in parallel, and what is the
fewest number of rounds?" Process in levels (BFS layers). Detect and print one cycle: DFS with colours.
In a real build system the pairs arrive incrementally; discuss incremental cycle detection.

28190 2347 13089 28126 34769 29511a:T77b,# Worst Hop: editorial

**Pattern.** Tree diameter by a bottom-up DP (the longest downward path, combined at the path's highest node).

**Brute force.** Search from every service and keep the largest distance: O(n^2). Fine for the small tests, about
4 * 10^10 steps at the limit.

**Key observation.** Every simple path in a rooted tree has exactly one highest node `v`. From `v` the path goes
down into at most two different child subtrees. So the answer is the maximum over `v` of
"the two best downward branches under `v`, added together".

**State.** `down[c] + w(c)` is the longest path that starts at the parent of `c`, steps to `c`, and keeps going
down. For each node keep the two largest such values among its children (`top1`, `top2`, both `0` if absent).

**Transition and order.** The best path bending at `v` costs `top1[v] + top2[v]`. Pushing `top1[v] + w(v)` into the
parent's top-two finishes the node. Because `p_i < i`, visiting `v = n-1 .. 0` handles every child before its
parent, so there is no recursion and no stack-depth risk on a 2 * 10^5 chain.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Pitfalls.** Considering only paths through the root (the heaviest path can sit deep in a subtree). 32-bit sums:
`2 * 10^5` edges of `10^9` reach `2 * 10^14`. Recursing on a chain of 2 * 10^5 nodes (stack overflow). Keeping only
the single best child, which finds the deepest node instead of the longest path.

**Follow-ups.** Return the endpoints (store which child gave `top1`). Two BFS/DFS passes also find a diameter in a
tree with non-negative weights (farthest from any node, then farthest from that). Handle negative weights (the
two-pass trick fails; the DP still works if you allow a branch to be skipped). Find the tree's centre. In serving
terms: this is the worst-case latency budget between any two components, which sets a floor on how a health check or
a cross-region sync can be timed.

1c:T61a,# Peak Window: editorial

**Pattern.** Monotonic deque (sliding-window maximum).

**Brute force (O(n * k)).** Scan each window for its maximum. Correct, and the specification used to check
the fast solution; with `k` near `n / 2` it is about 10^10 steps.

**Key observation.** When a new reading `x` arrives, any older reading in the window that is `<= x` can never
be the maximum of a window again: `x` is at least as large and stays in every window that contains the older
one for longer. So keep only candidates whose values are **strictly decreasing** from front to back. The front
is then the current window maximum.

**Algorithm.** For each index `i`: pop from the back while the back value is `<= load[i]`; push `i`; if the
front index is `<= i - k` it left the window, so pop it; once `i >= k - 1`, print the front value. Store
indices, not values, so you can tell when the front expires.

**Complexity.** Each index is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n) time, O(k) space.

**Pitfalls.** Forgetting to evict the front (stale maximum). Storing values and being unable to expire them.
Using `<` instead of `<=` is still correct but keeps equal values (fine, just a longer deque). A running
maximum reset every `k` steps confuses overlapping windows. Reading 64-bit values with 32-bit ints.

**Follow-ups.** Window minimum: flip the comparison. Window median: two heaps with lazy deletion or an ordered
multiset. Maximum over a 2D sliding window: apply the idea along rows then columns. Streaming input: the same
deque works online with O(k) memory.

999973617 9999736171f:T9a8,# Steady Latency: editorial

**Pattern.** Ordered multiset with a median iterator (sliding-window median).

**Brute force (O(n * k log k)).** Copy each window, sort, read position `(k - 1) / 2`. Correct, and the
specification used to check the fast solution; with `k` near `n / 2` it is far beyond the time limit.
`nth_element` makes each window O(k), which is still O(n * k).

**Key observation.** The median is a fixed *rank*, not a fixed value. Keep the window sorted in a
`multiset`; then the median is the element at position `(k - 1) / 2`. When the window slides, one value enters
and one leaves, so that element's rank changes by at most one: a single iterator can follow it.

**Algorithm.** Build the multiset from the first `k` values and park `mid` at position `(k - 1) / 2`. For each
slide: insert the new value (equal keys land after existing ones); if it is smaller than `*mid`, it landed before
`mid`, so move `mid` back one. If the outgoing value is `<= *mid`, it sits at or before `mid`, so move `mid` forward
one *before* erasing; this also keeps `mid` valid when the outgoing copy is `mid` itself. Erase exactly one copy with
`erase(lower_bound(value))`.

**Complexity.** Each slide does one insert and one erase, both O(log k), and O(1) iterator moves: O(n log k) time,
O(k) space.

**Pitfalls.** `erase(value)` removes *every* copy, corrupting the window with duplicates. Erasing before moving
`mid` can invalidate it. Using `k / 2` instead of `(k - 1) / 2` gives the upper median for even `k`. An average is
not a median. Values fit in 32 bits here, but `long long` costs nothing and protects you if a follow-up sums them.

**Alternatives.** Two heaps (max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half) with lazy deletion and a
balance counter: same O(n log k), more bookkeeping, and it needs care to keep the sizes right when stale entries
sit at the tops. A Fenwick tree over compressed values with a rank query (binary descent) is O(n log n) and has no
iterator subtleties, which many people prefer under interview pressure.

**Follow-ups.** Sliding-window percentile (p99 latency): the same structure with a different rank, but the rank then
moves by more than one position, so use a Fenwick tree or an order-statistics tree. Streaming median with no
deletions: two heaps are enough. Approximate quantiles over huge streams: sketches (t-digest, KLL) trade exactness
for memory; say so when an interviewer asks about production dashboards.
